fixes.explanation: Right, friend, it's False. Gideon sent messengers throughout Manasseh, as well as Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali (Judges 6:35). Four places, not one. Gideon was NOT keeping that invite list small, and the text says they came up to meet him.

Nope, nothing in Gideon's ask has the fleece vanishing. He asks for dew only on the fleece, and for the ground to be dry (Judges 6:37). The text says he squeezed the fleece the next morning (Judges 6:38). A vanishing fleece wouldn't leave him much to squeeze.

That's the one, friend. The LORD said there were too many men “…lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” (Judges 7:2) That's His stated reason, plain as that. The credit belongs where it belongs.
Somebody in that crowd was ready to head out, friend. The text says twenty-two thousand turned back, but ten thousand remained (Judges 7:3). That's far from none. That's a LOT of feet heading home.

That's ten times too many, friend. The text says the men who lapped with their hands to their mouths numbered three hundred (Judges 7:6). All the others knelt to drink. I'd have counted twice myself, and I'd still get three hundred.

Still too high, friend. The number who lapped the water with their hands to their mouths was three hundred (Judges 7:6). All the others knelt to drink. If I were counting, I'd ask for a recount, and I'd get the same answer.

That one belongs to the second night, friend. This morning, Gideon wrung out a bowlful of water from the fleece (Judges 6:38). The dry fleece comes after he asks again (Judges 6:39 and 6:40). Keep the nights straight and you're golden.

You got it, friend. The LORD said, “…go down to the camp with your servant Purah and listen to what they are saying.” (Judges 7:10 and 7:11) Then Gideon's hands would be strengthened to attack the camp. The LORD gave him a way to go down and hear for himself.

Calling the people back from home isn't the option, friend. The text says Gideon sent the rest of the Israelites to their tents (Judges 7:8). The LORD's other option was to go down to the camp with his servant Purah and listen to what they were saying (Judges 7:10 and 7:11). That's the one He gave.

Gideon doesn't hide behind his men, friend. The LORD told him to go down to the camp with his servant Purah and listen to what they were saying (Judges 7:10 and 7:11). Then his hands would be strengthened to attack. Sending the three hundred in without him isn't in the offer.

A stone would make sense for knocking over a tent, friend. But the man said he saw a loaf of barley bread come tumbling into the Midianite camp (Judges 7:13). It's bread, plain and simple. Of all the things to roll into a camp, a loaf is quite the pick.

A storm would be dramatic, friend, but that isn't what the dream meant. The man's friend said it was the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite (Judges 7:14). God had delivered Midian and the whole camp into Gideon's hand. Storm talk never comes up.

That's right, friend. Each man got a ram's horn in one hand and a large jar in the other, and inside the jar was a torch (Judges 7:16). A torch tucked inside a jar is a clever way to carry a light. Horn in one hand, jar in the other, busy hands all around.
It's True, friend. The text says the entire Midianite army fled, crying out as they ran (Judges 7:21). The word is entire, and the text means it. Not a handful, the whole army.

No hail in this story, friend. The text says the LORD set all the men in the camp against one another with their swords (Judges 7:22). It happened when the three hundred rams' horns sounded. Hail never comes up.

You got it, friend. Gideon told the men of Ephraim to “…seize the waters of the Jordan ahead of them as far as Beth-barah.” (Judges 7:24) So all the men of Ephraim were called out. And they captured the waters of the Jordan as far as Beth-barah.

That's right, friend. The men of Ephraim brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian, to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan (Judges 7:25). The text says they pursued the Midianites and then brought the heads to him. So Gideon was across the river.

Gideon isn't home, friend. The text says the men of Ephraim brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan (Judges 7:25). Ophrah isn't mentioned in this passage. The other side of the Jordan is where the text puts him.
